fact: Tom Allen opened a saloon in 1868 near the present Boatmen's Bank at Fourth Street and Washington Avenue, and was a tenant of the real estate firm J. C. Kaime & Bro. from then on.
Tom Allen was busy superintending the opening of a new saloon on Fitch Street, St. Louis, in March 1869.
The last $800 of stakes for the Allen and McCoole fight was put up at Tom Allen's saloon on 7 May 1869, and Allen attended to his saloon business in St. Louis until 10 May 1869.
Tom Allen's Concert Saloon was on Fifth Street between O'Fallon and Biddle streets in 1869, with a bar in front, a back room with tables and a piano, and a photograph of Allen over the decanters.
After the referee's decision on 15 June 1869, a crowd went to Tom Allen's saloon and the Concert Saloon was liberally patronized.
Tom Allen owned a saloon in June 1869, which the paper urged him to dispose of.
Tom Allen wrote to a St. Louis friend in August 1869 that he would buy Gallagher's business at a fair valuation and buy out other champions who wished to sell.
On 7 August 1869 $100 was deposited for a match at the Wash Home or at Tom Allen's saloon on Fifth Street, and Allen and Jim Coyne invited their friends to the saloon that evening.

The final stakes for the fight between Tom Allen and Charley Gallagher were deposited at Allen's saloon on 14 August 1869, with a crowd packed in while Allen, in first-rate condition, was there with his trainer Jim Coyne.
Stakes were put up at Tom Allen's saloon on 9 October 1869 before a large crowd, with Allen and Jim Coyne said to be present.
Jim Coyne held a levee at Tom Allen's saloon in St. Louis on 1 November 1869 and was welcomed by many friends.
After retiring, Tom Allen opened a saloon on Market Street near Seventh.
Tom Allen hosted a presentation of colors at his saloon to George Seddons of Boston on 19 January 1870.
Tom Allen's concert saloon and free-and-easy were at 417 Washington Avenue, between Fourth and Fifth streets, from 1870 to 1873.
Deposits for a match between George Seddons and Johnny Lafferty were to be made at Tom Allen's saloon in St. Louis.
J. L. Hughes, a Californian, left a $500 forfeit at Tom Allen's saloon for a challenge to fight at light weight.
A $100-a-side fight between Punch Morris and Steve O'Donnell was made up at Tom Allen's saloon on Saturday 6 August 1870, and its forfeit money was put up there.
John Madden said terms for a match with Buckey Barrett could be arranged by calling at Tom Allen's saloon.

Collins, the Cast Iron Man, wrote from a St. Louis saloon that he would put up $50 to $100 to meet Annabury, and invited Annabury's friends to make arrangements at Tom Allen's saloon on Saturday 20 August 1870.

The last preliminary deposit for the Allen and Gallagher fight was made at Allen's saloon on 24 October 1870, with John Campbell holding the stakes, and Roach put up $200 for Allen while Kelly put up $100 for Gallagher.
Tom Allen planned a grand opening of his new concert hall at 417 Washington Avenue on Saturday 4 March 1871, with concerts every Saturday, Sunday and Monday evening.

Jem Mace was Tom Allen's guest for three or four days before going to Kansas City to meet Joe Coburn in May 1871, and made Allen's saloon his favorite resort while training; Mace and Allen met their friends at the free-and-easy that June.
On the nights of 22 and 23 September 1873, Tom Allen's saloon and free-and-easy on Washington Avenue were crowded with fight followers, and Allen made a speech there telling the crowd to take a walk.
Tom Allen presided over his Saturday night 'free and racy' on 4 October 1873.
Betting at Tom Allen's Washington Avenue saloon on the night before the fight made him the strong favorite.
A Democrat reporter found Tom Allen in the back room of Allen's Saloon while asking for sporting news on 9 December 1873.

In February 1874 Tom Allen kept a hostelry on Washington Avenue by the tunnel in St. Louis; the Republican interviewed him there on February 19, and a Post-Dispatch reporter found Jack Madden there on February 24 while Allen was out.
From August to November 1874 Tom Allen's Free and Easy at 417 Washington Avenue was advertised as a place of amusement with the latest songs every night, with the champion keeping order.
On August 15, 1874, a large crowd gathered all day at Tom Allen's saloon, the Champion's Rest, and that night Allen kept order among the crowd at his Free-and-Easy, as was his usual custom.

In March 1875 Tom Allen's free and easy at 417 Washington Avenue had silver goblets displayed at its bar, and Allen announced he would take the chair there on Saturday night to sing his favorite songs.
In 1875 Tom Allen's saloon on Washington Avenue was called the Champion's Rest, and a reporter interviewed him in a rear room of it in May.
In June 1875 Tom Allen was found at his Free and Easy in the company of sporting men.
In July 1875 Tom Allen was well off financially and had a good business he was anxious to attend to.
In August 1875 a gambling game was running upstairs over Tom Allen's free and easy on Washington Avenue.
On September 29, 1875, a Globe-Democrat reporter called on Tom Allen at his saloon on Washington Avenue.

In December 1875 special officer Maloney seized a young man sitting in a chair in Tom Allen's saloon, and when the young man protested and Allen told Maloney to show his authority, Maloney drew a revolver in the saloon.
On February 22, 1876, Tom Allen's Gymnasium club held an entertainment in honour of Ned Donnelly.

In April 1876 Tom Allen closed his Free and Easy on Washington Avenue, and the counters and gin bottles were hauled out of the saloon; it was understood he would open another saloon at 611 Fifth Street in a few days.
About 1880 Tom Allen had been for about 23 years proprietor of a small saloon with an English concert hall annex on Market Street.
A gentleman who had backed Tom Allen in nearly all his old fights intended to set him up in business in St. Louis.
In March 1883 Tom Allen opened a saloon on Market Street between Sixth and Seventh, next door to Tom Kelly's and two doors from Jack Looney's.
On May 19 and 20, 1883, a sport at Tom Allen's saloon offered a reporter a good day's sport at the cock main the next morning.
In June 1883 Tom Allen advertised his concert hall, Champion's Rest, at 619 Market Street, open every evening with free singers and dancers and Allen in the chair.
On October 4, 1883, Tom Allen tried to light the street illuminations in front of his saloon, but the lights kept going out and he gave up in disgust.

On October 27, 1883, Tom Allen knocked out Jim Egan in a quarrel at his free-and-easy, and Egan and his friends were ejected; Allen pulled his pistol intending to kill Egan's dog, but put the revolver away.

On November 3, 1883, John L. Sullivan, with his manager Al Smith and some of his company, spent time in Tom Allen's Market Street saloon, where a large crowd gathered to look at him; his party retired to a room and drank champagne while Sullivan himself drank nothing.
On December 31, 1883, a wrestling match was held at Tom Allen's saloon.
In June and July 1884 Tom Allen advertised a free-and-easy every evening at his Market Street saloon at 619 Market Street, and entries for tournament events could be made at Allen's until July 2.

In late 1884 Tom Allen's saloon held free and easy concerts, Frank Rush, a coal miner, lodged over it as one of its regular attaches, and Allen was barely making a living running his concern on Market Street.
On September 4, 1885, Tom Allen was proprietor of a free-and-easy in St. Louis patterned after those in England, and he announced songs by rapping a gavel on the table.
In December 1887 Tom Allen advertised free concerts every evening at his place at 619 Market Street, where Smith and Kilrain's colors could be seen at the bar.
The day after the Flint fight, on 17 April 1888, a Post-Dispatch reporter interviewed Tom Allen at his saloon.
In May 1888 Tom Allen opened a boxing school at 619 Market Street, with a boxing ring in his saloon, joining a popular craze; it was to open that night with the finest singing in the city.

On 20 May 1888 Tom Allen's saloon closed at 12:40 a.m. under the midnight closing of the Sunday law; a policeman came in after midnight, spoke to the bartender, and the company in the back room broke up, while a bouncer knocked down a big man who objected to leaving and Allen led the bleeding man out.
In June 1888 Tom Allen kept a free-and-easy on Market Street, St. Louis.
On 20 January 1890 James St. John fell asleep in Tom Allen's saloon at 619 Market Street, St. Louis.
From February to August 1890 Tom Allen's saloon at 619 Market Street advertised a free concert every evening, with the best singers engaged.
On 25 July 1890 Lem McGregor knocked Tom Allen down in Tom Allen's saloon after a quarrel, and punished him to a considerable extent.
From September to December 1890 Tom Allen's place at 619 Market Street advertised a free concert every evening, with only the best singers engaged.
On 13 October 1890 Tom Allen was described as a saloon-keeper on Market Street.
From January to July 1891 Tom Allen's place at 619 Market Street advertised free concerts every evening with the best singers only.
In June 1891 Tom Allen kept a saloon on Market Street near Seventh Street in St. Louis.
From August to December 1891 Tom Allen's place at 619 Market Street advertised a free concert every evening, with only the best singers engaged.
In December 1891 Tom Allen ran a saloon on Market Street, in the same block as a saloon owned by Tom Kelly, a former middleweight champion.

From January to April 1892 Tom Allen advertised free concerts every evening at his place at 619 Market Street, St. Louis, with only the best singers engaged, and a reporter interviewed him there on March 5.
In May and June 1892 Tom Allen advertised free concerts every evening at 619 Market Street.

In July 1892 Tom Allen was still in the Market Street block between Sixth and Seventh streets, which was about to be torn down, and was advertised at 619 Market Street as the retired champion pugilist of the world.
From September to November 1892 Tom Allen advertised free concerts every evening at 619 Market Street, with only the best singers engaged.
In September 1892 Tom Allen kept a saloon in St. Louis called the Champion's Rest, and the championship cap of England was one of its revered ornaments.
In November 1892 Tom Allen's 619 Market Street saloon was called the Champions' Retreat, where Mark Tuohy was engaged as a song-and-dance performer and sparrer.
Dutch Niel said Charley Daly could see him at Tom Allen's place to talk business.
On November 25, 1892, William Reed, who had accepted Mark Tuohy's challenge at the Champions' Retreat, broke a window and cut Tuohy's head with a piece of the glass.
In December 1892 Tom Allen's place at 619 Market Street was advertised with a free concert every evening, with only the best singers engaged.
A sketch in Annie Bronson King's book The Children of the Slums opens at a place called 'Tom Allen's' on a Saturday night.
From January to July 1893 Tom Allen advertised free concerts every evening at 619 Market Street, St. Louis, with first-class singers engaged.
In early 1894 Tom Allen had a saloon on Market Street in St. Louis, the profits of which let him live comfortably.
In December 1894 prize fighter Jerry Slattery hung out around Tom Allen's saloon.
In January 1895 bartender Andrew Flynn struck Mathew Groves on the jaw in Tom Allen's saloon on Market Street near Seventh, slightly fracturing it.
In 1895 Tom Allen's saloon, Champion's Rest, was at 619 Market Street between Sixth and Seventh streets, St. Louis, and advertised a free concert every evening with the best singers.
From May to December 1896 Tom Allen's place was advertised at 619 Market Street, St. Louis, with a free concert every evening, and Allen was billed as the retired champion pugilist of the world.
On September 25, 1896 Tom Allen sat at a table with a mallet at Champion's Rest and called the frequenters to order to start a McKinley club.
In January 1897 Tom Allen ran a saloon on Market Street between Sixth and Seventh streets and a concert hall over which he presided every night.
From January to March 1897 Tom Allen's place was advertised at 619 Market Street, St. Louis, with a free concert every evening and only the best singers engaged.
In April 1897 Tom Allen ran his own place of amusement, a dance hall, on lower Market Street.
On April 27, 1897, after drinking at a party, Tom Allen found his saloon deserted and fired his gun to attract a crowd.
Denver Ed Smith, Paddy Smith and Ike Weir arrived in St. Louis, were lodged at Tom Allen's place, and held a reception there on Market Street on June 14, 1897, which ran until 2 a.m. Tuesday.
Mrs. Duffy sat at a window over Tom Allen's saloon, almost opposite the Ohio saloon, when an assault occurred on July 14, 1897.
Tom Allen was badly beaten in front of his saloon on Market Street, near Sixth Street, early in the morning of July 1, 1898.
From July 1898 to June 1899 Tom Allen's place was advertised at 619 Market Street, St. Louis, with a free concert every evening.
In November 1898 Tom Allen was at the Champion's Rest, around the corner from Tom Kelly's.

On September 5, 1899 Excise officers ordered Tom Allen's Market Street saloon to remove its wineroom; Allen said no woman had been in the place in six months, offered to take the door of his room off its hinges, and was left to construe the order after being told the penalty for disobeying it.
In 1900 Tom Allen was proprietor of the Champion's Rest, a concert hall in a Market Street building in St. Louis's Tenderloin, where he directed a concert nightly for his patrons.
In early 1901 Tom Allen owned the Champion's Rest saloon at No. 619 Market Street, St. Louis, a few doors east of Danny Daly's establishment.
Edward Hodo of Granite City fell down a flight of stairs at Tom Allen's saloon at about 1:40 a.m. on March 3, 1901.
Tom Allen conducted the Champion's Rest, a combined saloon and concert hall, in March 1903.
J. W. L. Gillespie acquired the Champion's Rest, a concert hall and saloon on Market Street formerly owned by Tom Allen, by a bill of sale given to him on Monday evening, March 30, 1903.
Mrs. Hartgrove had charge of the saloon during Tom Allen's illness and took charge of the money in the cash register, with power of attorney.
The Champion's Rest was headquarters of the Albion Social Club in April 1903 and was a resort for the city's poor, who could sleep in the chairs even with no money.
Gillespie paid $125 rent for Allen's saloon from April 1, 1903, and installed William Burns and his family in Allen's apartments above it to manage the place.

On April 2, 1903, Gillespie tried to take possession of Allen's saloon at 619 Market Street with a bill of sale made by Allen, who was sick; bartender John Murphy met him with a revolver, drove him out, and kept the day's receipts, acting on the advice of Robert Lyons, Allen's bartender for sixteen years.
On April 3, 1903, Gillespie came from Allen's room with an attorney and a notary, carrying a second bill of sale bearing Allen's mark.
On the night after Allen's death a yard of crape hung from the doorknob of his saloon, Tom Allen's Champion's Rest, at 619 Market Street, which was dark inside.

On April 6, 1903, W. A. Byrne, for Gillespie, claimed a bill of sale for the goods and fixtures and held the upstairs rooms of the Champion's Rest by force of arms if necessary, while John Murphy, Allen's bartender, refused to give up the bar, which he held for Allen's daughter.
Tom Allen's saloon at Market Street near Seventh had an old piano used at concerts, which the estate inventory listed in July 1903.
Jack Gillespie, a Klondike fortune-seeker, ran the Champion's Rest in August 1903.
